parrafos: Piedra del Águila (Eagle Rock) is one of the highest points of the Nahuelbuta Range (about 1,400 m a.s.l.), surrounded by araucaria trees inside Nahuelbuta National Park. This viewpoint offers unique views west to the Pacific Ocean and east to the volcanic chain of the Andes, particularly the Antuco, Sierra Nevada, Tolhuaca, Lonquimay and Llaima volcanoes.

The geosite is of great geological interest, as it is made of intrusive rocks of the Southern Coastal Batholith, 308 to 286 million years old, that is, Late Paleozoic (Carboniferous-Permian). The rock at the viewpoint is a granodiorite, made mainly of quartz, potassium feldspar and plagioclase, with inclusions of another dark rock up to 30 cm across, known in geology as xenoliths.

The magmas that formed the batholith are estimated to have cooled at a depth of about 12 to 15 km and to have had an initial temperature of 700 to 800 °C. Around the viewpoint there are also metamorphic rocks called gneiss, formed when sedimentary rocks were heated to very high temperatures (>600 °C) by the magma that produced the granodiorite.

The Navidad cone is a volcanic edifice 180 m high at the foot of Lonquimay stratovolcano, within the Nalcas National Reserve. It is one of several small eruptive centers aligned northeast-southwest for about 10 km, forming the Eastern Fissure Chain. It was built during the last eruption of the Lonquimay Volcanic Complex, between 1988 and 1990; this complex ranks 11th in the specific-risk ranking of Chile's active volcanoes (Sernageomin, 2023).

In December 1988, residents of nearby communities felt numerous earthquakes caused by rock fracturing. The Strombolian eruption began on December 25 of that year with an explosion whose column reached up to 9 km high, declining to about 2 km over the following months. Lava poured from the Navidad cone and flowed for 13 months down the Lolco River valley, reaching 10 km from its source. This offered a unique opportunity in Chile to describe and study a moving lava flow.

In addition, ash with a high fluorine content affected surface water, pasture and vegetation, causing osteofluorosis and the death of about 50,000 head of livestock. For this reason, residents of the town of Lonquimay, 25 km southeast of the cone, had to be evacuated.

The Truful-Truful Canyon geosite is in Conguillío National Park, within the Kütralkura Geopark. Here you can see the erosive power of the Truful-Truful River, which has exposed a 35 m wall recording part of the most explosive and violent history of Llaima volcano, one of Chile's most active volcanoes and ranked 3rd in the specific-risk ranking of active volcanoes (Sernageomin, 2023).

Although the volcano's historical eruptions have been relatively calm (Strombolian), with extensive lava flows, between 13,000 and 7,000 years ago (end of the Late Pleistocene to early Holocene) it produced highly explosive eruptions, recorded in the sequence exposed in the canyon. About 70 layers can be seen there, recording different volcanic processes during that period, such as ash fall, pyroclastic flows and surges, and volcanic mudflows (lahars).

At its base lies the product of the volcano's largest and oldest eruption, the Curacautín Ignimbrite. This large-volume deposit is associated with the collapse of the ancient Llaima volcano and the resulting formation of a caldera. The present volcano was built after this great eruption. The upper layers of the sequence, darker and about 3,000 to 4,000 years old, are deposits from the more recent and less violent activity of Llaima during the Holocene.

Villarrica volcano, or Ruka Pillañ (house of the spirit in the Mapuche language), lies southeast of Lake Villarrica and northeast of Lake Calafquén, with several towns at its foot, notably Pucón, with 28,523 inhabitants, only 15 km from its summit at 2,820 m a.s.l. With its almost perfect cone, recognizable from afar, it has a large summit glacier covering about 30 km2 and holding the equivalent of about 4 km3 of water.

It is one of the volcanoes with the longest historical record of eruptions in South America and is monitored in real time because of its high hazard and proximity to towns. For this reason it ranks 1st in the specific-risk ranking of Chile's active volcanoes (Sernageomin, 2023), which orders volcanoes by the risk they pose. It began erupting about 650,000 years ago, in the Middle Pleistocene, and has had many eruptions producing lava flows, pyroclastic flows and volcanic mudflows (lahars). The lahars have hit nearby towns hard, most devastatingly Coñaripe in 1964.

Villarrica has an open summit crater about 200 m across, with a continuous fumarole and an almost permanent lava lake, where changes in depth, frequent small explosions and surface solidification are common, making it a true natural laboratory. An open crater with a lava lake exists at only seven volcanoes in the world, which, together with its beauty and easy access, makes it a world-class attraction with about 17,000 visitors a year.

g38.nombre: Valdivia Interglacial Deposits at Fuerte Niebla
parrafos: Niebla Castle, better known as Fuerte Niebla, is in the town of the same name, 18 km southwest of Valdivia. Declared a Historic Monument in 1950, it was built in 1671 during the so-called defensive war against the Mapuche, when fortifications were raised in most Spanish settlements south of the Biobío River.

It was built with local materials, including flagstone, clay, alerce wood, straw and slate, as well as a type of hardened sand known locally as cancagua, plus imported lime and brick. Its battery and moat, carved into cancagua, made Niebla Castle a unique building of its kind.

The fort stands on a coastal cliff 40 to 50 m high, created by uplift of the Valdivia coast in the Late Pleistocene. Several layers of cancagua are exposed here, assigned to the Last Interglacial Deposits of Valdivia (Middle to Late Pleistocene), with at least three distinct groups of layers differing in content and sedimentary structures. They reveal three different environments linked to sea-level changes during that time: a beach and shallow marine platform, an estuary, and a coastal barrier with dunes and a river delta.

g39.nombre: Aa and Pahoehoe Lavas of Villarrica Volcano
parrafos: Villarrica volcano, or Ruka Pillañ (house of the spirit in the Mapuche language), is a stratovolcano in the Southern Volcanic Zone, on the border between the La Araucanía and Los Ríos regions. At its foot lie Lakes Villarrica and Calafquén and the tourist towns of Pucón, Lican Ray and Coñaripe.

The volcano has been active almost continuously from the Middle Pleistocene, about 650,000 years ago, to the present. Its historical record, covering the last 440 years, includes more than 60 eruptions, some calm with only lava emission and others much more violent and explosive. This geosite shows the reach and traces of a historical eruption, the one in 1971.

Here you can see lavas on the volcano's southwestern slope, in the Chaillupén stream, reached from Route 5 South by the paved road linking Loncoche, Lican Ray and Coñaripe. These lavas have rough, rope-like surfaces that change into irregular surfaces with sharp-edged blocks. The former are called pahoehoe lavas and the latter aa lavas.

They are 4 to 13 m thick and about 16.5 km long from their source to the Chaillupén stream, a distance the lava covered in just 48 hours. Lava flows are among the most common products of volcanic eruptions and, together with lahars and pyroclastic flows, are among the greatest hazards for areas near eruptive centers.

This geosite is a small volcanic edifice in a low-lying area east of Lake Ranco and south of Cerro Los Guindos. The Mirador cone is part of a group of at least 70 volcanic centers, including scoria cones, craters and maars, aligned in a northeast-southwest belt called the Carrán-Los Venados Volcanic Field.

The eruptive activity that built this field mostly postdates the last glaciations and is concentrated in the last 10,000 years, the Holocene. Three eruptions were recorded in the 20th century: the Riñinahue maar in 1907, the Carrán maar in 1955, and the eruption that formed the Mirador cone in 1979. The cone's last eruptive cycle took place between April and May of that year, when a prehistoric scoria cone, partly eroded and covered by forest, reactivated. The eruption produced pyroclastic material and three lava flows, with a total volume estimated at 9 million cubic meters.

The Carrán-Los Venados Volcanic Field is highly active and hazardous and could begin a new eruptive cycle within years or decades, so it ranks 6th in the specific-risk ranking of Chile's active volcanoes (Sernageomin, 2023). Lava flows, pyroclastic surges, lahars and pyroclastic fall could seriously affect nearby communities. However, this same situation makes the geosite of great scientific interest, since it would allow direct observation of how a volcano forms from its earliest stages.

The Pilauco paleo-archaeological site, discovered in 1986, is on Río Cachapoal street in the city of Osorno. Hundreds of fossils and dozens of chipped, polished and perforated stone artifacts found in layers of a swamp 16,400 to 12,700 years old help us understand the end of the Pleistocene, its inhabitants and the megafauna that lived there.

The fossils include gomphotheres (relatives of elephants), American horses, Hemiauchenia (ancestor of the guanaco), xenarthrans (relatives of the mylodon), Patagonian rats, antifer (marsh deer), coypus, pudús, skunks, deer and birds, as well as insects, pollen, seeds, wood, herbs and aquatic plants from this ancient swamp. The archaeological record includes a 15,600-year-old human footprint, the oldest recorded in South America so far, which would belong to a person weighing about 72 kilos and 1.82 m tall.

In addition, evidence of a meteorite impact in the area has led to the hypothesis that this asteroid may have caused the extinction of the megafauna 12,800 years ago, just as the dinosaurs are thought to have died out about 66 million years ago. The diversity of fossil fauna, pushing back to 20,000 years the date when humans entered the Americas, and a possible explanation for the megafauna extinction give this geosite invaluable scientific and educational value for Chile and the world. Some of the finds are displayed at the museum hall of Parque Pleistoceno Chuyaca, at 601 Santa María street in Osorno.

The Petrohué Falls geosite is on the river of the same name, 6 km from the outlet of Lake Todos Los Santos, and is one of the most visited attractions of Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park. The falls originated with lava flows that ran down the southeast side of Osorno volcano, currently ranked 8th in the specific-risk ranking of Chile's active volcanoes (Sernageomin, 2023), when the river valley was still filled with ice from the last great glaciation in this area during the Late Pleistocene, called the Llanquihue Glaciation.

These lavas blocked the valley of the ancient Petrohué River and, since then and to this day, have been worn down and sculpted by glacial ice and by the river's water, producing a series of falls and channels carved into the volcanic rock that give the place exceptional beauty. The lavas are estimated to be 90,000 to 30,000 years old, making them Late Pleistocene.

This remarkable geological feature is set in an extraordinary natural environment, part of the Temperate Rainforests of the Southern Andes Biosphere Reserve. Most of the park's forests are evergreen, dominated by canelo, coigüe, patagua and pitra. Wildlife includes pudú, puma, huillín or river otter, torrent duck, Magellanic woodpecker, red-gartered coot and ringed kingfisher, as well as two marsupials, the long-nosed shrew opossum and the monito del monte.

Chaitén volcano lies 10 km northeast of the town of the same name and has a caldera 2.5 km across holding a group of lava domes produced by its recent eruptive cycles. Although there is no chronological record of its early stages, recurrent activity is recognized over the last 15,000 years, from the Late Pleistocene to the present, with explosive events of varying size and the building and destruction of lava domes.

Its last eruptive cycle began violently on May 2, 2008. Although notable seismic activity had been felt beforehand, the lack of an instrument network made it impossible to link it to Chaitén volcano, so the explosive eruption came as a surprise. In the first days, eruption columns reached almost 20 km high, forcing the evacuation of Chaitén. The large volumes of volcanic ash that fell were then remobilized by heavy rains in the following days, generating volcanic mudflows (lahars) down the Blanco River valley that flooded and partly destroyed Chaitén.

The explosive activity gave way to lava domes growing inside the caldera. The instability of volcanic material accumulated over months caused successive dome collapses that produced pyroclastic flows reaching the outskirts of the town. Dome growth stopped by the end of 2009, ending the eruptive cycle.

This eruption led to the creation of Sernageomin's National Volcano Monitoring Network to watch the country's most dangerous volcanoes, including this one, which ranks 7th in the specific-risk ranking of Chile's active volcanoes (Sernageomin, 2023). The domes can be seen today from the town of Chaitén, with abundant steam degassing and rising temperatures.

This geosite is inside Cerro Castillo National Park, 7 km northwest of Villa Cerro Castillo. This massif beside the Carretera Austral reaches 2,318 m a.s.l. and stands out in the landscape for its rugged relief, colorful rocks, native forest and glaciers, which together invite contemplation.

The mountain is made of rocks of different origins and ages: mainly volcanic rocks of the Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous, marine sedimentary rocks of the same age, and intrusive magmatic rocks of the Late Cretaceous. The volcanic rocks, grouped in the Ibáñez Formation, come from violent eruptions here between 152 and 135 million years ago. At the end of that period volcanic activity ceased and gave way to a shallow sea where marine sediments were deposited; together with the volcanic rocks, they now form the mountain's rocks and make up the Coyhaique Group.

The intrusive rocks, part of the Patagonian Batholith, formed here about 98 to 93 million years ago from magma that cooled after penetrating the older volcanic and marine rocks. Tens of millions of years later, all these rocks were exposed at the surface and worn down and shaped, according to their hardness and resistance to erosion, by the ice of successive Pleistocene glaciations. This produced its steep, sheer pinnacles that look like the towers of a medieval castle and give this striking massif its name.

This geosite lies 5 km southeast of Puerto Río Tranquilo, on the shores of Lake General Carrera, and is reached by boat. Because of its extraordinary beauty it was declared a Nature Sanctuary in June 1994. Its rocks date from the Late Devonian-Late Carboniferous and belong to the Eastern Andean Metamorphic Complex. As the name suggests, marble is the main rock here, although there are also other metamorphic rocks known as calcareous schists.

Nearby you can also see a series of striking marble islands and rocks, which because of their shapes are called Elephant Rock, Dog's Head Rock and many other imaginative names. Both the marbles and the calcareous schists are made mainly of calcium carbonate. Water can dissolve this mineral and has been shaping these rocks for about 12,000 years, shortly before the start of the Holocene, forming columns, stalactites, stalagmites, caves, fractures and hollows.

The variety of minerals and crystal structures in the marbles and their arrangement in bands of different colors create their varied and intense coloring, enhanced by light reflected from the lake. The shapes, colors and banding of these rocks give this geosite incomparable beauty and make it a wonder of nature.

This geosite lies south of Lake General Carrera, in Lago Jeinimeni National Reserve, 25 km southwest of Chile Chico. Its rocks are remnants of volcanic deposits from violent, explosive eruptions during the Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous, about 152 to 142 million years ago. They belong to the Ibáñez Formation and represent the last volcanic episodes of that period in this region.

Piedra Clavada (Nailed Rock) is a pinnacle of volcanic rock about 40 m high and 6 to 8 m across, and one of the most striking examples of a series of columnar forms in the area. These forms exist because some zones of the volcanic rock were hardened by the addition of silica, making them more resistant to weathering and erosion. Thanks to fractures in the rock and to weathering by rain, ice, snow, wind and temperature changes, mainly during the Pleistocene and Holocene, these whimsical shapes were carved in the hardened rock and have survived over time.

The Paine massif, home to this geosite, crowns Torres del Paine National Park, a world-class tourist destination declared a Biosphere Reserve in 1978, 150 km north of Puerto Natales, in Última Esperanza Province. The range includes several prominent peaks, such as Paine Grande, the highest at over 3,000 m a.s.l.; the Cuernos (Horns) del Paine, rising between the deep glacial valleys of Bader and Francés; and the Torres (Towers) del Paine, three peaks about 2,600 m high and the most iconic rock formation of the reserve.

Besides the unusual shapes of the Towers and Horns, the Horns stand out for their two-tone coloring: a prominent white rock band with extremely flat, sharp contacts with the dark rocks that enclose it. The dark rocks are sedimentary layers revealing a deep sea during the Cretaceous, assigned to the Punta Barrosa Formation (Early to Late Cretaceous, about 105 to 93 million years old) and the Cerro Toro Formation (Late Cretaceous, 93 to 73 million years old).

The lighter rocks result from the intrusion of at least four granitic magma bodies which together cover 200 km2. These granites were emplaced about 13 million years ago, in the Middle Miocene, along a zone of crustal weakness called the Río Nutrias Fault. After millions of years buried, a series of tectonic uplift events fractured, deformed and raised these rocks above 2,000 m a.s.l., exposing them to erosion.

Then, during the Pleistocene, the rocks were heavily worked, according to their hardness and resistance, by glacial ice. The glaciers carved the unmistakable angular horns, cirques and ridges of this range, creating a magnificent landscape enriched by vast coirón grass steppes, running guanacos, flying austral parakeets, dense ñirre and lenga forests, and llareta cushion plants that live undaunted on the cold bare rock.

The Pali-Aike cone (desolate place in the Aónikenk language) is in the national park of the same name, 196 km northeast of Punta Arenas. It is part of the Pali-Aike Volcanic Field, an extensive volcanic plateau of more than 7,500 km2 in Patagonia, on the border between Chile and Argentina, with many volcanic landforms such as maars, tuff cones, scoria cones and lava flows.

This cone is a small volcanic edifice with a circular crater 160 to 180 m across, with steep walls (40-45° slope) that soften toward the base to slopes of 10-22°. It is horseshoe-shaped, open to the north, where a poorly preserved lava flow escaped. The Pali-Aike cone formed during eruptions between 130,000 and 17,000 years ago, in the Middle to Late Pleistocene. Although covered by vegetation and wind-blown sediment, its volcanic structures can still be recognized, as in many other eruptive centers in this field.

A volcanic cave preserved inside the cone, Pali-Aike Cave, adds to its cultural and scientific importance because of significant archaeological finds that have helped reconstruct the history of the early inhabitants of southern Patagonia. Evidence of human occupation, animal remains and stone and bone tools about 9,000 years old have been found there.

The Dientes de Navarino (Teeth of Navarino) geosite is an east-west chain of peaks in the center of Navarino Island, about 6 km south of Puerto Williams, the southernmost city in the world. These mountains are made of marine sedimentary rock layers of the Yaghán Formation, 130 million years old (Early Cretaceous), and intrusive rocks called diorites, 100 million years old (Late Cretaceous).

The diorites are more resistant to erosion than the marine sedimentary rocks, so they form most of the summits of the Dientes de Navarino. This set of rocks was uplifted, fractured and deformed by the Alenghi fault about 85 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous.

The jagged rocky peaks of the Dientes de Navarino are remnants of intense abrasion between 300,000 and 14,000 years ago, in the Middle to Late Pleistocene, by the slow flow of glacial ice loaded with rock fragments. Glacial erosion also left U-shaped, broad-floored valleys across the island and in these mountains.

Because of its extraordinary beauty and unique ecosystems, the island was added to the heritage routes of the Ministry of National Assets in 2001 and declared part of the Cape Horn Biosphere Reserve in 2005, which has helped protect and showcase this geosite at the end of the world.
